qin-shi-huang: Qin Shi Huang was born in Handan, the capital of Zhao, in 259 BCE as Ying Zheng or Zhao Zheng. According to the Shiji of Sima Qian, he was the eldest son of the Qin prince Yiren, a hostage at the court of Zhao who later became King Zhuangxiang of Qin. The Shiji also claims that he was the actual son of the merchant Lü Buwei. Modern scholars, among them Derk Bodde, doubt this and think the story was added to slander him.

King Zhuangxiang died in 246 BCE and was succeeded by his 13-year-old son. Lü Buwei acted as regent until 235 BCE, when Zhao Zheng assumed full power after Lü was banished for his involvement in a scandal with Queen Dowager Zhao. Lao Ai's attempted coup of 238 BCE failed, and Li Si became the new chancellor.

By 221 BCE he had conquered all the other warring states and unified China, and he took the new title huángdì rather than reuse the existing title for king. With Li Si he organised the empire into 36 commanderies, later 40, then counties, townships and hundred-family units, with appointments based on merit instead of hereditary right. They standardised weights and measures, the length of wagon axles and the currency, which became the Ban Liang coin, and the seal script of Qin became the standard for a universal written language. His public works included a national road system and the incorporation of the walls of several states into a single Great Wall.

He eliminated the Hundred Schools of Thought, and Legalism became the mandatory ideology. He is traditionally said to have banned and burned many books and executed scholars, and he fell ill and died during his fifth tour of eastern China.

The emperor died in July or August of 210 BCE at Shaqiu, aged 49. He had never written a will. Li Si and the eunuch Zhao Gao concealed his death, then forged a letter commanding his eldest son Fusu to commit suicide, and his younger son Hu Hai became the Second Emperor. His mausoleum, begun in 215 BCE, is guarded by the Terracotta Army.

Traditional Chinese historiography portrayed him as a brutal tyrant. Since the mid-20th century scholars have questioned this view, which stems partly from the harsh assessments of the Han dynasty that followed the Qin.
qizilbash: The name comes from Turkish and means red head, after a crimson cap of twelve gores which marked adherence to the Twelve Imams and to Shaykh Haydar, head of the Safavid order. It began as a pejorative used by their Sunni Ottoman enemies and was taken up as a mark of pride. In the 15th century Haydar organised his followers into militant troops. They were at first drawn from seven Turkish-speaking tribes: the Rumlu, Shamlu, Ustajlu, Afshar, Qajar, Tekelu and Zulkadar. Their beliefs were heterodox: they regarded their Safavid leader as a manifestation of the divine, and orthodox Twelver Shia classed them as ghulat, extremists.

By the summer of 1500 about 7,000 supporters had rallied to the young Ismail at Erzincan. They overcame a force of 30,000 Aq Qoyunlu and took Tabriz. In 1510 the Qizilbash defeated the Uzbeks at Marv, but in 1512 an army was destroyed at the Battle of Ghazdewan after Turcoman Qizilbash mutinied against their Persian commander, Najm-e Thani. On 20 August 1514 the Ottoman sultan Selim I, whose army had firearms and cannon and was reported to outnumber them as much as three to one, defeated them badly at Chaldiran. The defeat destroyed Ismail's belief in his own invincibility and changed his relation to his followers.

For almost ten years afterwards rival Qizilbash factions fought for control of the kingdom, and the ten-year-old Tahmasp I, who succeeded in 1524, was at first the ward of the Qizilbash amir Ali Beg Rumlu. Tahmasp reasserted his authority, and the Qizilbash defended the kingdom against Uzbeks and Ottomans until the Peace of Amasya in 1555. Abbas I, who came to power in 1588, built a standing army and administration from Circassian, Georgian and Armenian ghulams and ended the independent rule of Turcoman chiefs in the provinces. By the end of his reign a fifth of the high-ranking amirs were ghulams.

The Qizilbash remained part of the Safavid army and administration, and the Afshar and Qajar rulers who followed the Safavids came from a Qizilbash background. By the 18th century the name was applied broadly to anyone in the service of the Safavid state. Many Qizilbash were settled in Kabul and Kandahar during the conquests of Nader Shah, and others joined the Mughal court. In Afghanistan the Qizilbash live mainly in cities such as Kabul, Kandahar and Herat; estimates of their number range from 30,000 to 200,000.
quran: Muslims believe the Quran was revealed orally by God to Muhammad through the angel Gabriel over some 23 years, ending in 632 CE, the year of his death. Islamic tradition relates that the first revelation came in 610 CE in the Cave of Hira, on the Laylat al-Qadr, during one of his retreats to the mountains. According to tradition, several of Muhammad's companions served as scribes. Shortly after his death the Quran was compiled on the order of the first caliph, Abu Bakr, by companions who had written down or memorised parts of it. The caliph Uthman, who reigned from 644 to 656, established a standard version, the Uthmanic codex, which is generally considered the archetype of the Quran known today.

Some scholars argue that manuscript evidence, textual variants such as the Sanaa manuscript, and historical sources suggest a more gradual and complex process of compilation. Some textual critics hold that there never was a single original text, and Sunni and Shia accounts of its origins differ. Canonical variant readings, the qirāʾāt, are transmitted orally and differ only slightly in wording.

The text has 114 chapters, called sūrahs, made up of verses, called āyahs. The most popular Hafs version has 6,236 verses. The chapters are not in chronological order but roughly in order of decreasing size, and each except the ninth begins with the Bismillah, 'In the name of God'. Traditional accounts classify chapters as Meccan or Medinan, depending on whether they were revealed before or after Muhammad's migration to Medina.

The content covers basic beliefs such as the existence of God and the resurrection, narratives of earlier prophets, ethical and legal subjects, events of Muhammad's time, charity and prayer. Its style is allusive: events are referred to but not narrated, and people and places are mentioned but rarely named. For this reason Muslims rely on tafsir, or commentary, to explain it, together with the hadiths, oral traditions believed to record the words and actions of Muhammad.

In prayer the Quran is recited only in Arabic, ideally with a special prosody called tajwid. A person who has memorised the whole text is called a hafiz. Before printing was widely adopted in the 19th century it was copied by hand. The earliest manuscripts were in Hijazi script, and Kufic scripts with thicker strokes probably appeared in the ninth century. From the 11th century naskh, muhaqqaq and rayḥānī styles dominated, with the Maghribī style popular in North Africa and Iberia. Because copies were costly, they were often kept in mosques, frequently as a series of 30 parts, and Ottoman copyists were highly productive. Translating the text has always been considered difficult, since an Arabic word may have a range of meanings depending on context.
